entries.title: Grafana Tempo 3.1 Adds Query-Based Trace Redaction and Sampling-Aware TraceQL Metrics
entries.summary: Grafana Labs has released Tempo 3.1, the first minor update to the 3.0 architecture. It adds TLS and additional SASL mechanisms to the Kafka client, lets operators redact traces with a TraceQL query instead of a list of trace IDs, and introduces an experimental query-time hint that corrects TraceQL metrics for sampled data. By Claudio Masolo
entries.content:
Grafana Labs has released Tempo 3.1, the first minor update to the 3.0 architecture. It adds TLS and additional SASL mechanisms to the Kafka client, lets operators redact traces with a TraceQL query instead of a list of trace IDs, and introduces an experimental query-time hint that corrects TraceQL metrics for sampled data. vParquet5 also becomes the default block format. According to Grafana, simple metrics queries now run close to twice as fast.

The release builds on Tempo 3.0, published in June, which made the Kafka-compatible architecture (codenamed Project Rhythm) the default for microservices deployments. In that design, distributors write to a Kafka topic. Block-builders consume the topic to write Parquet blocks to object storage, and live-stores consume it to serve recent traces. Ingesters and compactors are gone, replaced by a backend scheduler and workers. Grafana says dropping replication factor 3 reduces storage from 3 to 3.5 times the trace volume to a single copy. Monolithic mode remains Kafka-free.

Because Kafka is now on the critical path, the 3.0 client's limits became a problem. It supported only SASL 

PLAIN
over an unencrypted connection, so any broker requiring TLS refused it. Tempo 3.1 adds TLS, including optional mTLS, plus 
SCRAM-SHA-256
, 
SCRAM-SHA-512
, 
OAUTHBEARER
, and 
AWS_MSK_IAM
. A new 
client_rack
option enables rack-aware fetching (KIP-392), so block-builders, live-stores, and metrics-generators can read from a replica in their own availability zone and avoid cross-zone transfer charges. It requires brokers with rack IDs configured. A new 
producer_compression
option accepts 
none
, 
gzip
, 
snappy
, 
lz4
, or 
zstd
; unset, it defaults to snappy. Grafana notes that this, together with TLS, makes Azure Event Hubs usable as a backend, since it accepts only gzip. All three changes came from community contributors.

Trace redaction, introduced in 3.0 through t`empo-cli redact`, previously required enumerating trace IDs. Sensitive values such as tokens or account numbers often appear across more traces than can practically be listed. In 3.1 the command takes a TraceQL query and supports 

--dry-run
, which counts matches without modifying blocks. Grafana limits the syntax to one spanset filter. It uses equality comparisons on 
resource.*
and 
span.*
attributes, along with 
&&
and 
||
. This is because the rewrite cannot be undone. 
--start
and 
--end
flags narrow the time range, which matters because Tempo pauses compaction for a tenant while a redaction applies. Grafana warns that older workers ignore the window and remove every match in each block they receive, without an error. The flags should only be used once every scheduler and worker runs 3.1.

TraceQL metrics, which became generally available in 3.0, gains three changes. The experimental hint with 

(extrapolate=true)
scales by the sampling rate in 
tracestate
. This follows OpenTelemetry's probability sampling rules. At 50% sampling, each stored span counts as two. Spans without a recorded rate count as one, so partial adoption does not distort other services. It applies to: 
rate
, 
count_over_time
, 
sum_over_time
, 
avg_over_time
, 
histogram_over_time
, 
quantile_over_time
, and 
compare
, but not to 
min_over_time
or 
max_over_time
. It requires vParquet4 or later and reads the rate the same way as the metrics-generator's 
enable_tracestate_span_multiplier
setting from 3.0, so ad-hoc queries and pre-aggregated series should agree. Second, +, -, *, and / now work between metrics queries and scalars, so an error rate becomes a single query. Third, the span-only fetch path, experimental in 3.0, is now on by default for vParquet5 blocks. In one warmed-up test, 
{ } | rate()
finished in slightly over half the time.

Other additions include an experimental span pruning option on the trace-by-ID v2 endpoint, which collapses similar leaf spans into one summary span carrying count and duration statistics. The same endpoint gains TraceQL filtering. A new experimental POST /api/v2/traces/diff endpoint compares two traces and can return a compact summary instead of a span-level patch. It is exposed through gcx, tempo-cli, and the Tempo MCP server, where Grafana says the smaller payload helps LLM-driven investigations. The metrics-generator gets an 

unmatched_span_kind
label on expired service-graph edges, support for the renamed OpenTelemetry db.system.name attribute, and pooled label buffers that Grafana reports reduce per-span allocations to zero in its service-graph benchmarks.

entries.title: Article: Server-Side DPoP and Token Exchange in Spring Security 7
entries.summary: Spring Authorization Server now lives inside Spring Security 7 under the same Maven coordinates, so the upgrade is a version bump. This server-side guide covers enabling DPoP and RFC 8693 Token Exchange, explains why 7.1 apps can silently stop enforcing DPoP until they call .dPoP(), and shows how to combine both into narrowed, sender-constrained tokens for service-to-service and agentic calls. By
entries.content:
Key Takeaways

  • Spring Authorization Server now lives inside Spring Security 7 under the same Maven coordinates, so moving off 1.5.x is a version bump, rather than an artifact swap.
  • Demonstrating Proof of Possession (DPoP) (RFC 9449) already worked end-to-end on Spring Security 6.5 with Spring Authorization Server 1.5. The real news on the 7.1 line is that resource-server verification is no longer automatic, so an app that relied on the old auto-applied behavior silently stops enforcing DPoP after upgrading until it adds the new 
    .dPoP()
    call.
  • Spring binds the JWK thumbprint via 
    cnf.jkt
    and the refresh token for public clients on its own, leaving two real decisions to the identity provider: the nonce policy and whether the 
    jti
    replay cache, which defaults to an in-memory, single-node implementation, needs to be swapped for a distributed one across a cluster.
  • RFC 8693 Token Exchange turns the bespoke "service-account swap" many identity providers (IdPs) still carry into a standard grant, with 
    subject_token
    and 
    actor_token
    semantics and an `act` claim that records the delegation chain.
  • The two features are more useful together than apart, because a DPoP-bound subject token exchanged for a narrowed, audience-restricted downstream token is the pattern service-to-service and agentic architectures keep reaching for, but the combined pattern is only as safe as the exchange policy and token customizer you write.

Your in-house identity provider has run on Spring Authorization Server 1.x for two years. The upgrade to Spring Boot 4 looks routine on paper. You bump the Bill of Materials (BOM), fix the deprecations, and ship it. Then you open the migration guide and find that the authorization server you depend on is no longer a separate project. It moved into Spring Security 7.0 while you were on the 1.x line. On the current 7.1 line, paired with Spring Boot 4.1, the two OAuth 2.1 features you have been deferring, sender-constrained tokens and a real delegation grant, are sitting in the same module, Spring General availability (GA) release, waiting to be switched on.

This is the part of the Spring Boot 4 migration that the migration guides skip. They cover Jackson 3, the lambda DSL, and the package relocations, then stop at OAuth 2.0. The auth-layer payoff is DPoP (RFC 9449) and Token Exchange (RFC 8693), both are production-ready in official components for the first time, which is where the upgrade actually earns its keep for anyone running their own IdP. This article is the server-side walk-through, covering what has been consolidated, what changes when you turn DPoP on, what an RFC 8693 exchange looks like end-to-end, and why the two features are worth running together. It assumes you already run an OAuth 2.0 / OIDC server and know the protocol. It does not re-explain OAuth from scratch.

What Spring Boot 4 Consolidated

Spring's November 2025 release train shipped in three steps: Spring Framework 7.0 on November 13, Spring Security 7.0 on November 17, and Spring Boot 4.0 on November 20. The release notes lead with modularization, JSpecify null-safety, API versioning, and the Jackson 3 baseline. The OAuth server story sits underneath these modules The changes had been announced two months earlier.

On September 11, 2025, the Spring team announced that Spring Authorization Server, a standalone project since 2020 and GA since November 2022, was moving into Spring Security 7.0. The standalone 1.5.x branch is the last generation with new development happening inside Spring Security. Spring Security shipped 7.1.0 in June 2026, paired with Spring Boot 4.1, then 7.1.1 in August 2026, so the current coordinates are 

org.springframework.security:spring-security-oauth2-authorization-server:7.1.1
. The consolidation itself happened at 7.0. The examples here target 7.1.1 specifically, because that is where both version-specific details this article covers land: the resource-server 
.dPoP()
opt-in (new in 7.1.0) and the pluggable 
jti
replay cache, which were new in 7.1.1 Each is called out where it appears. For a team that has been treating "the authorization server" as a separate dependency with its own release cadence, the consolidation is the headline. There is now one security module, one version, and one set of release notes to track.

There is a subtlety here worth getting right, because it is the single most common thing people get wrong about this migration. The Maven coordinates did not change. The standalone project was already published under 

org.springframework.security:spring-security-oauth2-authorization-server
and the merged module in Spring Security 7 uses the same groupId and artifactId. Only the version moved from the 1.5.x line onto the Spring Security version line (7.0.x, now 7.1.x). If you read somewhere that you need to rename a 
spring-authorization-server
artifact, that artifact never existed. One genuine rename does apply if you pull the authorization server in through the Boot starter rather than the library directly. In Boot 4, the starter gained a security- prefix, so 
spring-boot-starter-oauth2-authorization-server
is deprecated in favor of 
spring-boot-starter-security-oauth2-authorization-server
with both still published through 4.1.1. Beyond that, the migration is a version bump plus the same package relocations. Jackson moves every Spring Security 7 consumer absorbs. It is not a coordinate swap.
Xml


    org.springframework.security
    spring-security-oauth2-authorization-server
    1.5.7




    org.springframework.security
    spring-security-oauth2-authorization-server
    7.1.1

By moving to the 7.x line you inherit a module where DPoP issuance, refresh-token DPoP binding, and Token Exchange already coexist with the resource-server DPoP support that reached GA in Spring Security 6.5. Before this consolidation, getting all of those in one place required pinning a specific standalone authorization server version to a specific Spring Security version and hoping the matrix lined up. Now it is one version number.

Figure 1. The Spring Boot 4 consolidation. (Source: created by author.)

As shown in Figure 1, the standalone Spring Authorization Server (1.5.x, last generation) folds into the Spring Security 7.x line under the same Maven coordinates, consolidating DPoP and Token Exchange into a single module.

The Migration Tax, Paid Once

Before any of the new features, Spring Security 7 charges a baseline migration tax that is mostly not OAuth-specific: 

and()
is gone from the 
HttpSecurity
builder, Jackson 3 replaces Jackson 2, and a couple of JSON Web Token (JWT)-decoder defaults change. Spring's own migration guide and its OAuth 2.0-specific page walk through the mechanics; the concrete steps are items 2 through 4 in the playbook below.

The guide does not spell out two things, because they are specific to running an authorization server rather than any Spring Security app. First, the 

typ
header change is not a loosening of validation. Rather, it is Spring finally wiring in automatically what the 6.5 preparation steps asked you to add by hand: 
validateTypes(false)
turning off Nimbus's own 
typ
check so you could register 
JwtTypeValidator.jwt()
yourself and in 7.0 both halves of that dance happen for you. The actual audit point is narrower than "will my tokens still validate?". 
JwtTypeValidator.jwt()
requires 
typ
to be 
JWT
or absent, so any token your server issues or accepts with a different 
typ
, such as the RFC 9068 
at+jwt
access-token type, now fails validation by default unless you register a validator that allows it. Second, if you persist 
OAuth2Authorization
objects to a database with Spring's Jackson modules, that registration has to move from the Jackson 2 
SecurityJackson2Modules
to the Jackson 3 
SecurityJacksonModules
in the new 
org.springframework.security.jackson
package, or deserialization of previously persisted authorization state will break.

A team that is already up to date with Spring Security 6.5 deprecations can plan the baseline migration as roughly a one-sprint effort before touching any new OAuth 2.1 features. A team several versions behind should treat the baseline migration and the feature adoption as two separate efforts.

DPoP, End-to-End

DPoP (RFC 9449) constrains an access token to a key the client holds. The client generates an asymmetric key pair and, on each request, signs a short-lived proof JWT. The authorization server validates that proof at the token endpoint and binds the issued access token to the proof's public key. The resource server then refuses to honor the token unless it arrives with a fresh proof from the same key. A stolen token is inert without the private key. That is the whole point and it is the subject of this article's browser-side companion, which addresses the hard problem of where a browser can safely keep that key. Here the concern is the other end of the wire, namely what the server does when the proof arrives.

The proof itself is specified in RFC 9449 §4.2. The header carries 

typ: dpop+jwt
, an asymmetric alg, and the client's public key inline as a jwk. The payload binds the proof to the request with htm (HTTP method), htu (target URI, query and fragment stripped), iat, and a unique jti. When the proof accompanies an access token to a resource server, it also carries the base64url SHA-256 hash of that token.

Figure 2. The DPoP loop, server side. The authorization server binds the token to the client's key, and the resource server refuses it without a matching proof. (Source: created by author.)

Issuance: Two Decisions the Defaults Leave to You

On the authorization-server side, Spring wires the proof-verification machinery for you. 

DPoPProofVerifier
and the supporting 
DPoPProofJwtDecoderFactory
perform the RFC 9449 §4.3 checks: a well-formed JWT, a typ of dpop+jwt, a non-none asymmetric alg, a signature that verifies against the embedded jwk, and htm/htu matching the token request. Two things that look like decisions aren't. What is actually left to you is building the nonce challenge yourself (if you want it at all) and the reach of the replay cache.

The 

cnf.jkt binding is handled for you
. The access token must carry a 
cnf
claim whose 
jkt
member is the base64url-encoded JWK SHA-256 Thumbprint (RFC 7638) of the proof key. Spring populates this key automatically when DPoP is in play; the only thing to watch for is a token customizer that overwrites 
cnf
by accident. The resource server later compares against the thumbprint, not the public key and not a certificate hash.
JSON
{
  "sub": "service-a",
  "aud": "https://orders.internal",
  "cnf": {
    "jkt": "0ZcOCORZNYy-DWpqq30jZyJGHTN0d2HglBV3uiguA4I"
  }
}

First, consider the nonce challenge, which Spring does not implement at all. RFC 9449 §8 lets the authorization server demand a server-chosen nonce inside the proof, which stops a client from pre-minting proofs; the resource server has the parallel mechanism in §9. When a server requires a nonce the client did not supply, it answers with error: 

use_dpop_nonce
and a DPoP-Nonce response header, 400 at the authorization server, and 401 at the resource server. As of Spring Security 7.1.1, none of that exists in Spring's DPoP code on either side: no issuance of a DPoP-Nonce header, no handling of 
use_dpop_nonce
, and no validator checking the proof's optional nonce claim. The nonce challenge is a SHOULD in the RFC, not a MUST, which is presumably why it has shipped without one, but if your threat model needs it, you are building the entire mechanism yourself: issuing nonces, returning the challenge response, storing what you issued, and validating the claim against it.

Also Handled for You: Refresh-Token Binding for Public Clients

RFC 9449 §5 requires that when a public client presents a DPoP proof at the token endpoint, the refresh token it receives is bound to that key, and later refreshes must prove the same key. Spring Authorization Server added this key automatically in the 1.5.0-RC1 milestone (April 2025) and carried it into the 7.x line; there is no switch to flip. Confidential clients lean on their existing client-credential binding instead, so this approach matters most for single-page apps (SPAs) and native apps.

Second, there is the replay cache. RFC 9449 §11.1 requires rejecting a proof whose 

jti
has already been seen, within an acceptable time window. On Spring Security 7.0.x and 7.1.0, that check was hard-coded: a fixed, thousand-entry in-memory cache buried inside 
DPoPProofJwtDecoderFactory
, with no way to swap it out. Since Spring Security 6.5.12 / 7.1.1, it is the pluggable 
DPoPProofReplayValidator
, wired by default with its own InMemoryCache (one hundred thousand entries, capped per key). That default implementation's own Javadoc says plainly that it "only works in a single-node setup" and names Redis and Hazelcast as the kind of distributed Cache a clustered deployment needs to supply instead.

Verification Is Now Stock at the Resource Server

The resource-server side is where Spring 7 removes the most custom code. DPoP-bound access-token verification arrived through the Spring Security 6.5.0 milestones and went GA in 6.5.0 (May 2025). One version detail matters here. In Spring Security 7.0 that support was applied automatically whenever the DPoP classes were on the classpath, with no DSL hook. Spring Security 7.1 added an explicit 

dPoP(Customizer)
method to the resource-server DSL (@since 7.1), making support opt-in and customizable; in 7.1, you call 
.dPoP()
to enable it. This is a genuine behavioral change on upgrade, not just a new option: an application that relied on the auto-applied verification in 6.5 or 7.0, including one built entirely on Spring Boot's default resource-server autoconfiguration, which never called the new hook either, silently stops enforcing DPoP the moment it moves to 7.1 until 
.dPoP()
is added explicitly. A DPoP-bound token arrives under the DPoP authentication scheme, not Bearer. Sending it as Bearer is a common and incorrect shortcut. Spring's DPoPAuthenticationProvider does the work.

One naming trap is worth flagging, because it will bite during code review. The resource-server provider is 

DPoPAuthenticationProvider
, with no OAuth2 prefix, unlike 
OAuth2TokenExchangeAuthenticationProvider
in the next section. The converter and provider also live in different packages. 
DPoPAuthenticationConverter
sits in 
...resource.web.authentication
, while 
DPoPAuthenticationProvider
and 
DPoPAuthenticationToken
sit in 
...resource.authentication
, without the web.
Java
// Resource server: accept DPoP-bound access tokens.
@Bean
public SecurityFilterChain resourceServer(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    http
        .authorizeHttpRequests(authorize -> authorize.anyRequest().authenticated())
        .oauth2ResourceServer(oauth2 -> oauth2
            .jwt(Customizer.withDefaults())   // validates the access token
            .dPoP(Customizer.withDefaults())  // validates the proof: signature, htm/htu, ath, cnf.jkt
        );
    return http.build();
}

With 

.dPoP()
configured, the resource server verifies the proof signature, confirms htm/htu against the incoming request, checks that the proof's path equals the hash of the presented token, and confirms the proof key's thumbprint equals the token's 
cnf.jkt
. Before Spring Security 6.5 this was hand-written filter code. Now it is one line in the DSL.

Token Exchange Without the Bespoke Plumbing

Most in-house IdPs carry some version of "service-account swap". Service A needs to call service B on behalf of a user, so it reaches for a second set of credentials, mints a fresh token through a side channel, or passes the user's own token downstream and hopes the audience checks are lenient. RFC 8693 replaces that approach with a standard grant.

Token Exchange landed in Spring Authorization Server 1.3.0-M3 (March 2024) and is in the 7.x module. The grant type is 

urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange
. The request includes a 
subject_token
, the token representing the party on whose behalf the call is made, and an optional 
actor_token
representing the party acting, along with the audience, resource, and scope the caller wants on the way out.
Http
POST /oauth2/token HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
DPoP: eyJ...                     # the edge service's proof, so the issued token re-binds to its key

grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange
&subject_token=eyJ...            # the incoming user token, on whose behalf the call is made
&subject_token_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token
&actor_token=eyJ...              # the edge service's own token; this is what produces the act claim
&actor_token_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token
&audience=https://orders.internal
&scope=orders:read

The exchange matters most for the two semantics that RFC 8693 §1.1 distinguishes. Impersonation issues a token that appears to be the subject and the actor disappears. Delegation preserves both identities, the issued token carries the subject and an act (actor) claim identifying who is acting. Which one you get is decided by a single parameter. Send only a 

subject_token
and Spring's 
OAuth2TokenExchangeAuthenticationProvider
issues an impersonation token with no act claim. Send an 
actor_token
alongside it and the provider builds a delegation token, deriving the act claim from the 
actor_token
rather than from the authenticated client. For anything you will need to audit later and for service-to-service calls, delegation is exactly what you want.

RFC 8693 §4.1 represents a multi-hop chain by nesting act claims, with the outermost being the current actor and each nested one a prior actor. The nested entries come from the subject token. If the gateway's earlier exchange already left an act claim on the token the edge service now presents as its 

subject_token
, Spring carries that prior actor through as the nested entry. So in this example, edge-service, the actor token's owner, becomes the current actor, and gateway-service is nested beneath it as the earlier one.
JSON
{
  "sub": "user-123",
  "aud": "https://orders.internal",
  "scope": "orders:read",
  "act": {
    "sub": "edge-service",
    "act": {
      "sub": "gateway-service"
    }
  }
}

On the Spring side, the grant is handled by the 

OAuth2TokenExchangeAuthenticationProvider
, which is registered through the authorization-server configurer. The grant is not enabled by default per client. The calling client's 
RegisteredClient
must declare it, or the provider rejects the request with 
unsupported_grant_type
.
Java
RegisteredClient.withId(UUID.randomUUID().toString())
    .clientId("edge-service")
    // ... client authentication, scopes ...
    .authorizationGrantType(AuthorizationGrantType.TOKEN_EXCHANGE)
    .build();

The act claim, itself, is the framework's job, built from the actor token as described above, so you do not assemble it by hand. What is left to you is narrowing the issued token by dropping scopes or switching the audience, which is the job of an 

OAuth2TokenCustomizer
bean, the same hook you would use for any claim shaping.
Java
@Bean
public OAuth2TokenCustomizer tokenCustomizer() {
    return context -> {
        if (AuthorizationGrantType.TOKEN_EXCHANGE.equals(
                context.getAuthorizationGrantType())) {
            // Narrow the audience and trim scopes on the exchanged token.
            context.getClaims().audience(List.of("https://orders.internal"));
            context.getClaims().claim("scope", "orders:read");
        }
    };
}

One principle is worth holding on to. The exchange is where you reduce authority, so never widen it. A token-exchange endpoint that can be leveraged to access a broader scope than the subject token holds is a privilege-escalation bug, not a feature.

The Pattern That Needs Both DPoP and Token Exchange

The two features are each useful alone. Composed, they cover a problem neither closes by itself: propagating constrained authority across a chain of services without handing every hop a bearer token it could replay.

Picture an edge service that receives a DPoP-bound access token from a client. It needs to call an orders service on the user's behalf, but it should not forward the user's token wholesale. That token's audience is the edge and forwarding a bearer copy gives the orders service something it can, in turn, replay anywhere. Instead, the edge service performs a token exchange. It presents the user's token as the 

subject_token
, its own token as the 
actor_token
, and a DPoP proof on the exchange request, then asks for a token scoped to orders:read, audience https://orders.internal. The authorization server issues a narrowed token, records the edge service in the act claim from that actor token, and, because the edge sent a proof, binds the new token to the edge service's own key through 
cnf.jkt
.

Figure 3. DPoP-bound token exchanged for a narrowed, re-bound downstream token. Scope shrinks, audience switches, the actor is recorded, and each hop is sender-constrained. (Source: created by author.)

The result is concrete. The orders service receives a token it can verify is sender-constrained to the caller it is actually talking to, scoped to exactly what that call needs, with an audit trail of who delegated to whom. No hop holds a replayable credential for a service it does not call. This is the shape that modern service meshes and agentic systems keep reinventing badly with ad hoc header passing. RFC 8693 plus RFC 9449 are the standards-track versions and Spring Security 7 is the first official Spring surface where both halves ship together.

There is a real caveat. The narrowing is yours to enforce. Spring gives you the grant and the customizer hook, but it does not stop you from writing an exchange that widens scope or skips the audience switch. The security of the pattern lives in the 

OAuth2TokenCustomizer
you write. That code deserves its own tests.

A Migration Playbook

Two starting points cover most teams. The first is Greenfield on Spring Boot 4.1. A new IdP starts on the 7.x module with DPoP and Token Exchange available from day one. The work is configuration, not migration: register clients, decide your nonce policy, write the narrowing customizer, and turn on 

.dPoP()
at every resource server. Treat the 
OAuth2TokenCustomizer
as security-critical code from the first commit.

The second starting point is an existing standalone Authorization Server 1.5.x. This is a version bump on coordinates you already use, not a re-platforming. The sequence:

  • Move to the Spring Boot 4.1 / Spring Security 7.1 BOM. Bump spring-security-oauth2-authorization-server from 1.5.x to 7.1.x, same groupId and artifactId.
  • Convert any remaining 
    and()
    -style filter chains to the lambda DSL.
  • Audit 
    JwtDecoder
    configuration for validateTypes(false) and confirm the new 
    JwtTypeValidator
    defaults accept your tokens.
  • Update Jackson module registration where you persist authorization state, so 
    SecurityJackson2Modules
    becomes 
    SecurityJacksonModules
    .
  • Only then, as a separate change, enable DPoP for new client registrations and stand up the token-exchange grant, after the baseline migration is green.

The production rollout has its own decisions. The decisions that turn a feature flag into a deployment. Keep the issuer URL stable across the cutover. Advertise DPoP and the token-exchange grant in the authorization-server metadata so clients can discover them. Roll out resource-server 

.dPoP()
support before you start issuing DPoP-bound tokens, so the verifier is ready when the first bound token arrives. Plan a dual-stack window in which bearer and DPoP-bound tokens coexist as clients migrate. Enable DPoP per client registration rather than globally, so the existing fleet keeps working while new registrations opt in.

The metadata is what lets clients discover all of this functionality. The authorization server's 

/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server
document should advertise both capabilities: the DPoP signing algorithms it accepts and the token-exchange grant in its grant-type list.
JSON
{
  "issuer": "https://idp.internal",
  "grant_types_supported": [
    "authorization_code",
    "refresh_token",
    "urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange"
  ],
  "dpop_signing_alg_values_supported": ["ES256", "RS256"]
}

What Comes Next

Watch the nonce gap specifically. The RFC marks it a SHOULD, not a MUST, and there is no open feature request for it in Spring Security's issue tracker as of this writing, so an identity provider that wants it is building it alone and should plan for that rather than wait on a future release.

The more durable trend sits a level above this one release. Multi-hop service calls and increasingly chains of autonomous agents acting across trust boundaries need both proof of key possession and an audited, narrowing delegation chain, not just a bearer token and a scope check. RFC 8693's nested `act` claim already models that chain. As that architecture spreads, the pairing this article covers, DPoP binding plus token exchange, looks less like a Spring Security 7 feature pairing and more like a default expectation for identity providers generally.

References

  • RFC 9449, OAuth 2.0 Demonstrating Proof of Possession (DPoP), IETF, September 2023.
  • RFC 8693, OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange, IETF, January 2020.
  • RFC 7638, JSON Web Key (JWK) Thumbprint, IETF, September 2015.
  • "Spring Authorization Server is moving to Spring Security", Spring blog, September 11, 2025.
  • "Spring Framework 7.0 General Availability", Spring blog, November 13, 2025.
  • "Spring Boot 4.0.0 available now", Spring blog, November 20, 2025.
  • Spring Security 7.0.0 release, GitHub, November 17, 2025.
  • Spring Security Reference, OAuth 2.0 DPoP-bound Access Tokens.
  • Spring Security issue #16940 / PR #17202, "Add support dpop customization" (dPoP(Customizer), @since 7.1).
  • "The DPoP Storage Paradox: Why Browser-Based Proof-of-Possession Remains an Unsolved Problem", InfoQ, April 2026 (companion article).

entries.title: Meta Extends Confidential Computing to AI Glasses with Private Processing
entries.summary: Meta has extended Private Processing to AI glasses, using confidential VMs, trusted execution environments, remote attestation, anonymous credentials, OHTTP routing, and TEE-based storage to process AI workloads and persistent user context in the cloud. By Leela Kumili
entries.content:
Meta has extended Private Processing to AI glasses, using confidential virtual machines (CVMs) for sensitive AI workloads and persistent user context in the cloud. The design combines Trusted Execution Environment (TEEs), remote attestation, anonymous credentials, OHTTP, and encrypted storage. Meta says it supports streaming transcription, contextual search, and long-term recall requiring more computing and persistent state.

Basic interactions, such as calls and messages, can run on the glasses, while more advanced workloads require larger models and access to personal context accumulated over time. Meta introduced Private Processing for WhatsApp and Meta AI in 2025 and is now extending the architecture to wearable AI workloads.

Oskar Linde, VP of XR Technologies at Meta, described the approach on LinkedIn as a way to make AI more useful throughout the day while supporting the stateful, personal context required by AI glasses without allowing Meta to access that data.

The architecture moves the confidential computing boundary from the device into Meta's cloud infrastructure. AI models run inside confidential virtual machines (CVMs) backed by hardware TEEs, with processor encrypted memory. Meta says the boundary spans CPUs and GPUs, allowing mixed workloads to remain protected.

Before transmitting personal context, the glasses perform remote attestation and establish an attested TLS session with a TEE. The device verifies a hardware-signed certificate and compares the workload measurement against an append-only transparency ledger. Failed verification prevents data transmission. Anonymous credentials and third-party OHTTP relays operated by Fastly or Cloudflare further separate user identity from request processing.

Meta's Private Processing architecture (Source: Meta Blog Post)

Persistent state remains inside the confidential boundary. Meta places the storage engine inside the TEE and encrypts data with user provided keys before it leaves the protected environment. Queries execute within the same boundary, limiting exposure of database access patterns.

Private Processing is built around hardware isolation, fail closed guarantees, public verifiability, non targetability, and encrypted storage. Production CVM images are registered in the transparency ledger. Because engineers cannot inspect protected memory or capture model inputs and outputs, Meta relies on aggregate operational signals such as CPU utilization, memory allocation, network latency, and hardware failure rates.

The privacy implications of always on wearable AI have also generated community discussion. In a Reddit discussion about Meta's glasses, one commenter argued that an assistant providing contextual information would need to continuously listen and observe its surroundings, highlighting the privacy implications of persistent sensing.

Deployment remains a limitation. WIRED reported that Private Processing is not yet available on Meta's glasses, and Meta has not specified which features will initially use the system or provided a timeline for its availability. Meta engineering director Pritam Shah said the platform is ready and working, but that Meta was announcing it before broader deployment to engage security and privacy researchers and a third party auditor.

Meta says it is working with independent security firms, including NCC Group, and security researchers to review the architecture and attestation mechanisms. The company also plans to provide researchers with CVM binaries, tools, and documentation as it expands the system for increasingly stateful, multimodal, and agentic AI experiences.

entries.title: Presentation: How to Find Resilience Bugs in Systems that Don't Exist
entries.summary: Hillel Wayne discusses how formal methods principles - such as property strength, state-space verification, and environment assumptions - help software engineers uncover critical architectural bugs early. He shares practical mental models like "adversarial non-determinism" to reason about concurrency, edge cases, and distributed system failures without needing complex mathematical tools. By Hillel
entries.content:
Transcript

Hillel Wayne: I have a bit of a weird job. Companies pay me to find bugs in systems that don't exist, or more specifically, don't yet exist. They come to me with some idea for a system they want, but they're also afraid the system might lose them customers if it goes wrong, and they ask me to look at their description and tell them if there's a really bad bug somewhere. Growing up in extreme programming and agile shops, this felt verboten to me when I first started doing it. After all, we all know that we can only find bugs at the very end when we have the whole coding system that we can test, possibly in production. It's actually a relatively simple process that all of us can do. To show you that this is just even possible in the first place, let's walk through the thing doer.

The thing doer does a thing. It first checks to see if the thing has been marked done. Then it marks the thing as done. Then it actually does the thing. Would anybody like to shout out the problem with this thing doer? Yes, there, you found a bug in something that didn't exist. The problem with this is that we all know this is not how an actual system works. The actual system is going to look like this. Doing the thing might fail. If it fails, we have to retry. If we retry, we get to this point where we check the thing is marked done, and see, it's been marked done. Then we just never do the thing. That's a bug. Properties

Let's start with what it means for a system to be correct. To formalize this notion, we have the idea of a property. A property is something that should be true of a working system. If it is false, then the system is wrong in some way and needs to be fixed. Properties, notably, are Booleans. They are either true or false. They are not partially true. An example of a property is that we have 99.999%, five nines of uptime. This is something that is verifiably true or false. If we are down for more than five-and-a-half minutes a year, our system does not have this property and we need to make a more sophisticated system or migrate cloud providers, depending. This is a property. It is also a relatively complex property that is hard to verify. We are often interested in automatically verifiable properties that we can easily check.

An example of this might be that all the messages we send in our system follow the appropriate schema. I would recommend checking out Ian Cooper's talk. That is some of the things he was talking about, the ways of enforcing this property in his systems. Properties get much more detailed than that or much more low level. Even something like a unit test is a property. Testing that max of 1, 2, 3 as 3 is the property that a given input always gives a certain output. If your system does not give that output for that input, something is wrong and must be fixed. Our thing doer had two properties that we talked about at failing. We don't do the thing more than once. Or a safety property, something bad that we want to prevent. We do the thing at least once. Or liveness, something good that we want to make sure happens.

I said that properties are Booleans. This leads to a very interesting consequence. Take the property that a system can handle 10,000 queries per second. Think of the set of every possible system you could build that to some degree of abstraction satisfies this property. Now take the property of can satisfy two queries per second, every possible system that can satisfy two queries a second. The set of properties that can satisfy 10,000 queries is a strict subset of those that can satisfy 2 queries. If a system can satisfy 10,000, it can satisfy 2. We would say that being able to satisfy 10,000, having this property, implies you have this property too or implication. This is an extremely useful thing that comes out of mathematics.

Some other examples of properties that satisfy this is that if you have no memory errors, this implies you have no use-after-free errors. If you have exactly once delivery somehow, you have at least once delivery and also at most once delivery. Something like GDPR compliance implies that you have cookie banners on every page of your site. Notice that these properties on the left-hand side are harder to satisfy than the properties on the right-hand side. Also, if you know you have the property on the left-hand side, you automatically have the one on the right-hand side. This gives us a notion of property strength. The properties on the left-hand side are stronger than the ones on the right-hand side. Some properties are stronger than others, and this is really important for verification. Because if we have a property that is strong and we know it's satisfied, like a test that a user can buy something with a coupon, if this passes, we automatically know the system has all the weaker properties too.

You can apply coupons and you can complete orders. If you run this test and it passes, you don't even need to run these tests hypothetically. The other consequence is actually more important, the consequence of the contrapositive. Notice in this space that there are three distinct regions. The region that satisfies both 10,000 and 2 QPS, the region that satisfies 2 but not 10,000, and the region that satisfies neither. There is no region that satisfies 10,000 QPS but not 2 QPS. If 10,000 implies 2, 2 not holding implies 10,000 doesn't hold either. If a system breaks at 3 queries a second, it's clearly not going to handle 10,000. This is called the contrapositive and leads to something quite interesting. If we have a set of weaker properties and we know one isn't satisfied, like you can't actually add shipping, we don't even need to look at the stronger property, we know it doesn't hold either.

If you're trying to figure out what's wrong with your system, which is more helpful, knowing that this test fails or knowing that 70 of these tests pass and this one fails? It is pretty much universal that strong properties passing show that a system is correct, while weak properties failing show why a system is incorrect. This actually explains a lot of practice in how we verify systems. Think about the testing pyramid. Environment

This brings me to the last aspect of this talk, environment. Environment is all the assumptions that need to be true for our system to work. In the first version of the thing doer, we need the assumption that the system never crashes to guarantee liveness. This may or may not be a good assumption, but it probably is one we have to have. Even think of something like trying to click a clicker. You have to assume it always works because it is totally valid for it to have the error that you try to press a button, but before you do, it catches fire. Without the ability to say that things always make progress, you simply cannot have any properties at all. This still reiterates that properties are things outside of our control. Often, these assumptions come from other people's systems we don't have control over. If a vendor decides to switch from always consistent delivery of messages to eventual consistency, what can you do about that?

You can change vendors maybe, but you can't tell them to go back to the old behavior. This is a really defensible assumption. If we add in the fail state, we now need a much stricter assumption that do thing never fails. This is a lot less defensible. If I see a client say, "We're just going to make this assumption that this never ever fails". I'm going to be like, "Your system has a bug", just saying. This is something that might push us to using V2. In this case, in V2, we no longer need the assumption that do thing never fails. We could have a much weaker assumption, that do thing fails only a finite number of times. Even if we fail at this step a million times, we still, on the million and first, go past this. We're done. We have satisfied liveness. This kind of really fine-grained assumption is what formal methods is really good at. It really forces you to think about all the kinds of assumptions of so many different types that go into a system. I would also like to point out that do thing never fails and do thing fails only a finite number of times are very qualitatively similar properties, if not quantitatively.

This brings us back to strength and weakness. Some assumptions are stronger than others, just like some properties are stronger than others. No failures is a stronger property than finite failures. Strong consistency is a stronger assumption than eventual consistency. When we have stronger assumptions, we can have stronger properties for the same level of sophistication of our system. Correspondingly, weaker assumptions can be compensated by system design. One good example of this I think about is I used to work for a company where we knew for a fact that every single one of our users would stop using our software at 4:00 New York time. This made deployments extraordinarily easy. We could just turn off everything around 6 p.m., update it, and turn it back on. We had a very strong assumption that made it easy for us to guarantee deployment properties. Imagine Google doing the same thing.

Just imagine it. It would be very funny to imagine. Another thing, though, is that different systems require different levels of assumption for different properties. It's not monotonic. A system design doesn't make all properties necessarily easier to guarantee for the same assumptions. We see this in version 2 again. In version 2, we needed a weaker assumption to guarantee liveness but we need a stronger assumption to guarantee safety. We need to assume there is only one thing doer acting at a time. It might be possible for there to exist in V3 of the thing doer, where V3 does not require either of these strong properties. It might be able to work even with only finite failures, but also guarantee safety even if there's more than one thing doer. That system, if it exists, is probably going to be a lot more sophisticated than either V1 or V2.

I've found empirically that there's this relationship between sophistication of the system, the properties you want to guarantee, and the strength of the assumptions you have, where either one of these can be fixed and the other two change based on that. For example, if you wanted to guarantee liveness for the same level of assumption, of say a message being passed, like are all messages processed? You can actually do that, even with weak assumptions, by weakening the property. From all messages are processed to all messages are either processed or go into a dead letter queue. One of the other consequences of this is that weakening assumption often weakens the properties you have. Summary

In a summary of what I've talked about, systems have assumptions and properties. These can be related in terms of strength. Some properties are stronger than others, and some assumptions are stronger than others. For a given property and assumption, the system sophistication depends on both these things. A system needs to be more sophisticated to handle a stronger property, and needs to be less sophisticated given a stronger assumption. Strong properties show correctness. When they pass, we know our system is correct. Weak properties show incorrectness. They're used to debug why things are going wrong. We can look at a simplified model to find a real-world bug in the system. Then, finally, beware of the gremlin. I hate the gremlin.
